newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says he still backs Lake for CIA director.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says he still backs Lake for CIA director.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Thursday he stood firmly behind Anthony Lake, his nominee for director of central intelligence, and did not believe the nomination was threatened.
Asked during a White House event if he thought Lake's nomination was in trouble and if he would fully support him, Clinton replied, "No and yes."

CBS News reported on Wednesday that Lake was questioned last week by the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section about an apparently inadvertent failure to sell off more than $200,000 in energy stocks.

The White House said late on Wednesday Clinton was satisfied Lake made an innocent mistake in not complying with an order to sell the stocks to avoid a conflict of interest. "We reviewed that, and I believe the esseential facts of the matter have been reported in the press," Clinton said on Thursday. "We believe that it is not a disqualification."

Clinton appeared to be commenting on Lake's failure to sell the stocks rather than on concern expressed by a senior Republican senator on Wednesday about Lake's support of a 1994 policy that misled Congress on Bosnia.

Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania said he might oppose Lake, currently Clinton's national security adviser, over a 1994 policy on Iranian arms shipments that kept both Congress and then-CIA Director James Woolsey in the dark.
"I have great reservations about Mr. Lake and about his sensitivity, given what went on in this matter," Specter said at a final hearing for outgoing CIA chief John Deutch.

Specter was the second senior Republican senator in a week to question Lake's nomination. Pete Domenici of New Mexico said on Sunday Lake faced "tough sailing" in the Senate and called his replacement of Deutch "a kind of in-house coup."
But White House spokesman Mike McCurry played down the possiblity that Lake's Iran-Bosnia stance might pose a hurdle, saying the issue had been thoroughly reviewed.

"I think the items of concern there have been addressed by the administration and addressed by Mr. Lake on other occasions," McCurry said on Wednesday. "I am not aware that that should pose any significant problem."
As national security adviser, Lake was an architect of a policy giving Croatia a secret go-ahead to let Iranian arms reach Bosnian Moslems in violation of a U.N. embargo.
